inline_comments.comment: The PR description says the fix 'checks if the .js file exists; if not, tries TypeScript alternatives,' but the code does the reverse — TypeScript alternatives are always tried first, and `.js` is only used as a fallback. The code is correct for TypeScript's Node16/NodeNext resolution semantics, but this means that in a mixed codebase where both `./foo.js` and `./foo.ts` exist, importing `./foo.js` will silently resolve to `./foo.ts`. This is a silent behavior change that could break projects that genuinely have compiled `.js` files alongside their `.ts` sources. Consider documenting this preference explicitly, or checking whether the `.js` file actually exists before attempting the TypeScript redirect (only redirect if the `.js` file does NOT exist at all).

The comment cites the full TypeScript Node16 resolution order, including `.d.ts`, but the implementation never tries `.d.ts` candidates. This is intentional (`.d.ts` files aren't loadable source files), but a reader may expect the code to follow the comment faithfully. Revise the comment to describe what this code actually does: 'When a .js-extension import is used, check if a TypeScript source file (.ts/.tsx) exists at the same base path and prefer it, matching TypeScript's Node16 module resolution behavior.'

The file-level `directoryCache` (used by the extensionless resolution path) exists to avoid redundant filesystem probes. The new JS-to-TS path calls `existsSync` uncached on every import with a JS extension, once per candidate TypeScript extension. For projects with many imports, this can add up to a meaningful number of extra syscalls per HMR cycle. Consider whether the directory cache can be reused here, or at minimum cache the result so repeated resolution of the same `importPath` doesn't re-hit the filesystem.

The `.jsx` → `['.tsx']` mapping can cause unintended redirection. If a project has a genuine JavaScript JSX file `Button.jsx` alongside a `Button.tsx`, importing `./Button.jsx` will silently resolve to `./Button.tsx`. Unlike `.js`/`.mjs`/`.cjs` (which are also valid TypeScript output extensions), `.jsx` as a source file is more commonly an actual JavaScript file. Consider whether this mapping should be included, or at minimum add a code comment explaining the reasoning.

general_comments.comment: No unit tests are added for the new `resolveWithExtension` JS-to-TS code path. The PR checklist has no test boxes checked, and the explore agent's summary of the existing 6 `resolveWithExtension` tests does not include any that directly exercise the new branch (e.g., calling `resolveWithExtension('./vite-config.js', '/some/file.ts')` when `vite-config.ts` exists). Coverage via `addExtensionsToRelativeImports` tests is useful but not sufficient — direct tests for `resolveWithExtension` with `.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, and `.jsx` inputs (including the fallback-to-JS case when no TS alternative exists) are needed. Additionally, the old test 'Returns path as-is if already has extension' may now be incorrect since `.js` imports are no longer returned as-is; verify it was updated to reflect the new behavior.

The `jsToTsExtensionMap` constant is not exported. If tests want to validate the mapping directly (e.g., ensuring `.mjs` maps to `.mts` and not `.mts`/`.mtsx`), they currently cannot without going through the full `resolveWithExtension` function. Exporting it would make the mapping independently testable and allow consumers to extend it if needed.
